title: TIPP: Four Skills for When You're Too Distressed to Think
hook: When emotion is so intense you can't reason your way calm, a clinical psychologist's go-to is TIPP — four body-based moves that lower the intensity fast enough to think again.
key_points: TIPP stands for Temperature, Intense exercise, Paced breathing, and Paired muscle relaxation.
Cold on the face triggers the mammalian dive reflex, quickly slowing heart rate and panic.
Short bursts of intense exercise burn off stress chemistry the mind can't just talk away.
These are drawn from dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) — built for crisis-level distress, not everyday stress.
content_html: Standard advice like "just breathe" can fail when distress is intense enough to hijack clear thinking. A clinical psychologist points to TIPP, a set of four body-first skills from dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) designed to lower emotional intensity fast enough that you can think again.
extra_html: TIPP stands for Temperature, Intense exercise, Paced breathing, and Paired muscle relaxation. Temperature means cold — splashing icy water on your face or holding an ice pack there triggers the mammalian dive reflex, which slows the heart rate and eases panic within moments. Intense exercise, even a few minutes of jumping jacks or sprinting in place, burns off the stress chemistry flooding the body. Paced breathing — exhaling longer than you inhale — activates the parasympathetic nervous system. Paired muscle relaxation means tensing and releasing muscle groups in sequence to release physical tension. According to NPR, these skills are meant for moments of genuine crisis-level distress, not everyday stress, where gentler tools are usually enough.

related.title: Quick Ways to Calm Down
related.hook: When stress spikes, you can't think your way calm — but you can breathe your way there. A few simple tools work in minutes, anywhere.

related.title: What Stress Does to Your Body
related.hook: A jolt of stress is useful — it sharpens you for a real threat. The problem is when the alarm never switches off, and the body pays for staying on high alert.

flashcards.prompt: Why does dunking your face in ice water help during a distress spike?
flashcards.back_html: Cold on the face triggers the mammalian dive reflex, an automatic response that slows your heart rate and dials down panic — fast, and without needing to reason your way calm.

flashcards.prompt: What does the 'P' in TIPP's paced breathing rely on to calm the body?

choices.text: Holding your breath as long as possible
Breathing as fast and shallow as you can

flashcards.explanation_html: A longer exhale than inhale activates the parasympathetic ("rest and digest") nervous system, easing the body out of a stress spike.

flashcards.prompt: When are TIPP skills meant to be used, versus tools like slow breathing alone?
flashcards.back_html: TIPP is built for moments of crisis-level distress — so intense you can't think straight — not routine day-to-day stress, where lighter tools like calm breathing or grounding are usually enough.
